title: Response caching and output caching middleware
hook: Response caching stores whole HTTP responses using Cache-Control headers. Output caching (.NET 7+) is server-side middleware that caches rendered responses before they leave your API — faster than rebuilding JSON on every identical GET.

blocks.text: Response Caching Middleware honors HTTP caching semantics — ETag, Cache-Control, Vary — and can store 200 responses in memory on the server or let clients and CDNs cache. Output Caching (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OutputCaching) is a separate pipeline feature: you tag endpoints with policies, vary by query or header, and store response bodies in IMemoryCache or Redis without requiring clients to send cache headers. Both apply to safe GET/HEAD requests; neither replaces authorization checks before cache lookup.

entries.plainDefinition: Middleware that caches responses based on HTTP cache headers and request method.
Server-side response store with named policies, independent of client Cache-Control.
Opaque validator for conditional GET — If-None-Match returns 304 Not Modified.
Tells caches which request headers create separate cache entries.

blocks.text: Public catalog endpoints benefit from output caching when millions of identical GETs hit your API — you skip controller, service, and database work entirely on a hit. Misconfigured caching leaks one user's JSON to another (missing Vary on Authorization) or serves stale prices after updates (no invalidation). Interviews contrast HTTP semantics (CDN-friendly) with output cache policies (server-controlled TTL).

blocks.title: Auth and cache order
blocks.body: Cache lookup must happen only after authentication/authorization when responses differ by user. Default policies should not cache personalized endpoints unless Vary includes the right headers or policies key by user id.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Request enters pipeline
items.body: Routing matches endpoint with CacheOutput attribute or extension.

items.title: Build cache key
items.body: Policy combines route, query keys, vary-by headers, and optional tags.

items.title: Cache hit
items.body: Middleware short-circuits — returns stored status, headers, body.

items.title: Cache miss
items.body: Pipeline runs endpoint; response captured on way out.

items.title: Store with TTL
items.body: Entry expires per policy; EvictByTag on admin writes clears groups.

snippet.label: Register output caching with Redis store
snippet.explanation: AddOutputCache registers policies. UseOutputCache before MapControllers. Redis store shares output across pods — memory store is per process like IMemoryCache.

snippet.label: Response caching with Cache-Control for CDN
snippet.explanation: ResponseCacheLocation.Any allows CDNs to cache. VaryByQueryKeys prevents page=1 and page=2 collisions. Combine with output cache for origin shielding.

snippet.label: Invalidate by tag after admin update
snippet.explanation: Tag-based eviction clears all catalog policy entries without knowing every query combination — critical after bulk price updates.

snippet.label: Failure-mode — never cache authenticated routes without user key
snippet.explanation: Personalized output cache keys must include principal identity or tenant. Safer default: CacheOutput only on anonymous reference endpoints.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Caching POST responses. Missing Vary on Authorization for semi-public APIs. UseOutputCache after MapControllers (never runs). Stale admin data because no tag eviction on writes. Assuming response caching works without AddResponseCaching and UseResponseCaching.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: compare output cache hit ratio metric to origin CPU drop. X-Cache or Age response headers on CDN logs. After onboarding spike, if output cache hit rate stays low, keys may be over-varied (unique query per user). Application Insights dependency duration should drop on cached routes — if not, middleware order is wrong.

blocks.title: Response caching vs output caching
rows: Origin optimization; CDN still needs headers

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Caching authenticated order history without user-specific keys. Placing UseOutputCache after endpoints. Saying output cache replaces Redis data cache — they solve different layers (full HTTP response vs domain object).

interviewTakeaways: Response caching = HTTP Cache-Control semantics; output caching = server-side policy store (.NET 7+).
When not to use: mutating methods, personalized payloads without proper vary keys, or rapidly changing inventory without eviction.
Production tip: tag policies for EvictByTag on writes; Redis IOutputCacheStore for multi-instance farms.

60s: Output cache middleware checks policy key before endpoint runs — hit returns stored body. Response cache honors HTTP headers for CDN. Auth before cache for user-specific data. Invalidate tags on admin updates.
Follow-up: how do you cache a public GET but still return fresh data within five seconds after a write?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'we cache everything with [ResponseCache]' gets you rejected — personalized APIs need vary keys or no cache.
UseOutputCache registered after MapControllers — middleware never executes.
Strong answer: 'Anonymous catalog output-cached five minutes with catalog tag; EvictByTag on PUT; user dashboards use IMemoryCache not full response cache.'
introducedIn: Response caching since ASP.NET Core 1.0; output caching added in .NET 7

jsTsCorrelations.note: apicache stores responses in memory like output cache; Cache-Control header mirrors ResponseCache Location.Any for CDN.
fastify-cache wraps reply.send — similar short-circuit before handler on hit, but lacks built-in tag eviction.
